content: Sodium periodate refers to two distinct chemical compounds, both of which are sodium salts of the two types of periodate ions. Sodium metaperiodate, commonly abbreviated as m-periodate, has the chemical formula NaIO4. Sodium orthoperiodate, often abbreviated as o-periodate, has the chemical formula Na5IO6. These salts are particularly valuable in synthetic chemistry due to the oxidative properties of the periodate ion. The density of sodium periodate is 3,865 kg/m³, and it is soluble in water. Upon heating, sodium periodate decomposes to form sodium iodate (NaIO3) and oxygen gas. This decomposition reaction is catalyzed by manganese(IV) oxide. It is important to note that the correct pronunciation of periodate is per-eye-oh-date, not period-ate. Sodium periodate is utilized in the oxidation of cellulose to produce a biocompatible and biodegradable compound. This compound has applications as a suture material, a scaffold for tissue engineering, or as a medium for drug delivery. In solution, sodium periodate can cleave saccharide rings at vicinal diols, resulting in the formation of two aldehyde groups. This reaction is frequently employed to label saccharides with fluorescent molecules or other tags, such as biotin. Since this reaction specifically targets vicinal diols, periodate oxidation is often used to selectively label RNA, as ribose contains vicinal diols. In contrast, DNA, which contains deoxyribose, lacks vicinal diols and is not affected by this process.
